jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: A Recent Photo
jokes.joke: I lost my son at an amusement park. Security asked for a recent photo. I showed them a selfie of me eating a corn dog. The guard said, 'Where's your son?' I said, 'Zoom in on my sunglasses. You can see him walking away.'

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Cousin Dale's Business Plan
jokes.joke: My cousin called to borrow money. Said he's opening an amusement park. I said, 'Dale, you can't even keep a houseplant alive.' He said, 'That's why it's perfect. Nobody's coming back for a refund.' I asked what rides he had. He said, 'One. You stand in line for four hours and then I tell you it's closed.' I lent him forty bucks. That's the most honest business model I've ever invested in.

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: Family Budget
jokes.joke: I took my eight-year-old nephew to Six Flags yesterday, and by hour two, the financial power dynamic completely shifted. I paid sixty bucks just to park near the dumpsters, twenty-two for a bottle of lukewarm Dasani, and by three o'clock I was making direct eye contact with a third-grader whispering, 'Hey buddy... how much tooth fairy cash do you have in your Velcro wallet?'

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Wrong Line
jokes.joke: I'm so inattentive that last time I went to the amusement park, I waited forty minutes thinking I was next for the big roller coaster. Turns out it was the line for the restroom. The guy in front of me turns around and goes, 'You know this isn't a ride, right?' I said, 'With the pressure I'm feeling, it better have a bigger drop than Space Mountain.'

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: VIP Line
jokes.joke: I got hired to organize a birthday at an amusement park. The client said, 'Make the kids feel like VIPs.' I misunderstood and spent the whole budget creating a fast pass for the parents. By noon, every kid was crying, every adult was smiling, and honestly that's the closest I've ever come to a five-star event.

scores.comment: Clear premise with several comic turns, but the houseplant comparison is disconnected from the later gags. The closed-ride joke is familiar, and the final line explains the humor rather than delivering a stronger punch.

Strong escalation from recognizable amusement-park prices to an adult desperately soliciting a child's tooth-fairy savings. Specific details, believable frustration, and an effective final image. Slightly overwritten opening, but the payoff lands.

The mistaken queue establishes the premise, but the confusion strains credibility. The final bathroom-pressure and roller-coaster-drop connection feels forced rather than surprising, weakening the payoff.

Coherent setup and a relatable reversal prioritizing parents over children. The crying-kids, happy-adults contrast is amusing, but the final five-star-event observation is predictable and lacks a decisive punch.
Strong visual turn: the missing son appears in the sunglasses reflection, walking away. It's clear, economical, and the final image carries the laugh. The inattentiveness is shown, not announced.

Specific, relatable details (dumpster parking, $22 Dasani) build to a good role reversal: the adult hitting up a third-grader for tooth fairy cash. The last line lands, but the setup runs long and could be tighter.

The wrong-line mix-up is a familiar setup and 'I'm so inattentive that' is a stock opener. The restroom-pressure payoff is mildly amusing, but the Space Mountain comparison is a predictable toilet-humor turn.
The fast-pass-for-parents misread is a decent, fresh idea. The closer is weaker, because 'closest to a five-star event' is vague and softens the contrast of crying kids and smiling adults.
Terrific economy and stage rhythm. The reveal of zooming in on the sunglasses reflection lands with a sharp, genuinely funny visual punch.
A bit meandering with multiple mini-punchlines that dilute the impact. Competent premise, but feels like an extended sketch pitch rather than a tight stand-up bit.
Starts with an overt 'I'm so inattentive that' tell-not-show opening, followed by a very well-worn bathroom line premise and an awkward, strained tag.
Solid, clean logic and relatable parental schadenfreude, though the concluding tag wraps up a bit too quietly to generate a big laugh.
Tight premise and visual punch; solid but mild laugh.
Strong escalation and honest-business closer; genuine comic idea.
Vivid money-shift turn lands cleanly; familiar park-cost setup.
Clean inversion and final line carry; natural stage rhythm.
Strong visual and clear inattentive-parent angle; punchline is amusing but fairly predictable.
Good escalation from loan request to absurd business model; honest-investment tag lands well.
Specific details, clear escalation, and a strong image in the final turn; most memorable of the batch.
Solid structure and callback to ride drops, but the misunderstanding premise feels familiar and the payoff is mild.
